title: Contract Law Essentials
summary: Learn how contracts are formed, what terms mean, when agreements can be set aside, what remedies exist for breach, and how to review and manage contracts, with examples from African and common-law systems.
audience: Students, entrepreneurs, freelancers, managers and anyone who signs agreements

body.p: A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. Contracts are everywhere: buying airtime, renting a room, taking a job, hiring a builder, signing up for an app. Most do not need to be written down, but writing them helps prove what was agreed.

list: Agreement: a clear offer and an acceptance of that offer.
Intention to create legal relations: the parties meant to be legally bound (social arrangements between friends usually are not).
Capacity: the parties are legally able to contract; minors and people without mental capacity are protected.
Legality and possibility: the purpose must be lawful and possible to perform.
Certainty: the main terms (what, how much, when) must be clear enough to enforce.
In common-law systems such as Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and England, consideration: each side gives something of value.

body.p: Legal systems differ. South Africa follows Roman-Dutch common law, where consideration is not required and the focus is on serious intention and agreement. Some contracts must be in writing everywhere, such as the sale of land in many countries.

body.tip: This course explains general principles. For a real dispute or a high-value contract, take advice from a qualified lawyer in your country.

lessons.title: Offer, acceptance and forming the agreement

body.p: An offer is a definite promise to be bound on stated terms if the other side accepts. Many things that look like offers are only invitations to treat, which invite people to make offers: goods on a shop shelf, most adverts, price lists and online product pages. The customer makes the offer at the till, and the shop accepts it.

list: Acceptance must match the offer exactly. Changing a term is a counter-offer, which rejects the original offer.
Acceptance usually takes effect when it is communicated to the offeror. Silence is not normally acceptance.
An offer can be withdrawn before acceptance, unless the offeror promised to keep it open in return for something (an option).
Offers end when rejected, when a stated time passes, or after a reasonable time.

body.p: Clicking "I agree" or "Buy now" can form a binding contract if the terms were reasonably available. Electronic signatures are recognised in many countries, for example under South Africa's Electronic Communications and Transactions Act and Kenya's Information and Communications Act, though some documents still need handwritten signatures or witnesses.

body.tip: Before replying "yes, but" to an offer, remember that a changed term may cancel the deal you wanted.

body.p: Terms set out each party's obligations. Express terms are stated in words or writing. Implied terms are added by law, custom or the obvious intention of the parties: for example, that goods sold are of acceptable quality and fit for purpose, which consumer laws often guarantee.

list: Conditions or essential terms: breaking them can allow the other side to end the contract.
Warranties or minor terms: breaking them gives a right to damages only.
Payment terms: amount, due date, method and interest on late payment.
Exclusion and limitation clauses: try to limit liability; courts read them strictly, and consumer laws make some unfair ones invalid.
Termination clauses: how and when the contract can be ended.
Dispute resolution clauses: negotiation, mediation, arbitration or a named court.

body.p: Consumer protection laws, such as South Africa's Consumer Protection Act and Kenya's Consumer Protection Act, protect buyers from unfair, unreasonable or misleading terms.

body.tip: Read the payment, termination and liability clauses first; they cause the most disputes.

lessons.title: When a contract can be set aside

body.p: Sometimes an apparent agreement is not valid, or one party can escape it, because consent was not real or the contract is unlawful. These are called vitiating factors.

list: Misrepresentation: a false statement of fact that persuaded the other party to contract. Deliberate lies (fraud) give the strongest remedies.
Duress: consent obtained by threats of violence or unlawful pressure.
Undue influence: one person exploits a position of trust or power over another.
Mistake: in limited cases, a fundamental mistake shared by both parties, or about the identity of the subject matter, can make a contract void.
Illegality: contracts to commit crimes or against public policy are not enforced.
Lack of capacity: contracts with minors are often not binding on the minor, except for necessities.

body.p: Remedies can include rescission, which undoes the contract and returns the parties to where they were, and sometimes damages. Delay in acting after discovering the problem can lose the right to rescind.

body.tip: Keep copies of adverts, messages and promises made before you signed; they are evidence if a misrepresentation is later denied.

body.p: Breach happens when a party fails to perform as promised: late delivery, defective work, non-payment or refusing to perform at all. The innocent party may have several remedies.

Damages aim to put the innocent party in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed. If a supplier agreed to sell equipment for R100 000 but fails to deliver, and the buyer has to buy the same equipment elsewhere for R120 000, the basic damages are 120 000 - 100 000 = R20 000. Losses must be caused by the breach and not too remote, and the innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce (mitigate) them.

list: Specific performance: a court order to perform, used when money is not an adequate remedy, such as for unique property.
Termination: ending the contract for a serious breach.
Interest on late payment: R50 000 paid 60 days late at 10% a year simple interest adds 50 000 x 0.10 x 60 / 365, about R821.92.
Penalty or liquidated damages clauses: a pre-agreed amount for breach, usually enforced if it is a genuine estimate of loss rather than a punishment.

body.tip: Before suing, send a clear written demand stating the breach, what you want and a deadline; many disputes settle at this stage.

body.p: Clear contracts prevent disputes. Use plain language, define key words, and make sure the document matches what was actually agreed. Templates help, but adapt them to the deal and the law of your country.

list: Parties: correct legal names, registration numbers and addresses.
Scope: exactly what will be delivered, to what standard and by when.
Price and payment: amounts, currency, tax, deposits, due dates and late-payment interest.
Risk: warranties, liability limits, insurance and force majeure (events beyond control).
Duration, renewal and termination.
Confidentiality and data protection, where personal data is involved.
Governing law and dispute resolution.
Signatures, dates and attachments.

body.p: Store signed contracts safely, diarise renewal and notice dates, and record changes in writing as signed amendments. A dispute over a R30 000 job is often about scope: if extra work worth R2000 was agreed by phone but never written down, proving it is hard.

body.tip: If a clause would surprise or worry the other party, discuss it openly before signing; hidden surprises damage trust and may not be enforced.

quiz.q: Which is usually an invitation to treat rather than an offer?
options: Goods displayed on a shop shelf
A written promise to sell at a fixed price to a named person

quiz.q: A buyer replies to an offer, "Yes, but at a lower price." This is:
options: A counter-offer that rejects the original offer

quiz.q: Is silence normally acceptance of an offer?
Which requirement is needed in common-law systems such as Nigeria and Kenya but not in South African law?
A term implied by law into a sale of goods is usually that the goods:
options: Can be returned after five years
Are of acceptable quality and fit for purpose

quiz.q: Breaking a warranty (minor term) usually allows the innocent party to:
A contract made because of threats of violence is affected by:

options: Undoes the contract, returning parties to their original positions

quiz.q: Goods agreed at R100 000 are not delivered; a replacement costs R120 000. Basic damages are:
What is the duty to mitigate?
options: The court must reduce the price
The innocent party must take reasonable steps to reduce its loss

quiz.q: R50 000 is paid 60 days late at 10% simple annual interest. The interest is about:
When might a court order specific performance?
options: When money would not adequately compensate, such as for unique property

quiz.q: Why diarise renewal and notice dates?
options: It is required for all verbal contracts
To change prices without telling anyone
To avoid automatic renewals and missed deadlines
